The same data, four ways¶

Back to Worked Problems

Which fit is right depends on the question and on what is wrong with the data. This problem fits one data set with the four families of the guide and looks at what each gets right and wrong. The data are a positive quantity that grows exponentially with x, observed at 20 points with additive noise and one gross outlier:

y = exp(0.5 + 0.18 x) + noise, with the observation at x = 15 raised by 8.

The true mean curve is known, so each fit can be scored against it. The four fits are a straight line (ols_fit), a quadratic (poly_fit), the normal family with a log link (glm_fit), whose mean is exp(b₀ + b₁x), and the median line (quantile_fit).

The fits and their errors¶

The program prints each fit’s coefficients, the root mean square error against the true mean over x from 0 to 19 (the range of the data) and at the extrapolated points x = 25 and 30, and, where the likelihoods are comparable (the three that are Gaussian), the AIC.

#include <pluss/ma.h>
#include <pluss/tils/aux/output.h>

namespace reg = pluss::subsp::stats::regression;
using namespace pluss::tils;

int main() {
  OutputEngine out;
  out.print_defaults(PrintOptions{}.fixed(3));
  std::vector<double> xs, ys;
  for (int i = 0; i < 20; ++i) {
    xs.push_back(i);
    ys.push_back(std::exp(0.5 + 0.18 * i) + 0.6 * (2.0 * std::fmod(i * 0.6180339887498949, 1.0) - 1.0) + (i == 15 ? 8.0 : 0.0));
  }
  const auto x = pluss::make_series(xs, {20}, as_f64());
  const auto y = pluss::make_series(ys, {20}, as_f64());
  auto truth = [](double v) { return std::exp(0.5 + 0.18 * v); };

  const auto line = reg::ols_fit(y, x);
  reg::PolyOptions quadratic_options;
  const auto quadratic = reg::poly_fit(y, x, quadratic_options);
  reg::GLMOptions log_options;
  log_options.family = reg::GLMFamily::Normal;
  log_options.link = reg::GLMLink::Log;
  const auto exponential = reg::glm_fit(y, x, log_options);
  const auto median = reg::quantile_fit(y, x);

  const auto grid = pluss::make_series([] { std::vector<double> g; for (int i = 0; i < 20; ++i) g.push_back(i); return g; }(), {20}, as_f64());
  const auto at = pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{25.0, 30.0}, {2}, as_f64());
  auto rmse_to_truth = [&](const pluss::Series &predicted) {
    double sum = 0.0;
    const auto p = predicted.pull<double>();
    for (int i = 0; i < 20; ++i) {
      sum += (p[i] - truth(i)) * (p[i] - truth(i));
    }
    return std::sqrt(sum / 20.0);
  };
  auto extrapolation_error = [&](const pluss::Series &predicted) {
    const auto p = predicted.pull<double>();
    return std::vector<double>{p[0] - truth(25.0), p[1] - truth(30.0)};
  };

  out.writeln("truth at x = 25 and 30:", truth(25.0), truth(30.0));
  out.writeln("straight line      coefficients", line.coefficients.pull<double>(), " rmse to truth", rmse_to_truth(reg::ols_predict(line, grid)), " error at 25, 30", extrapolation_error(reg::ols_predict(line, at)), " AIC", line.aic);
  out.writeln("quadratic          coefficients", quadratic.ols.coefficients.pull<double>(), " rmse to truth", rmse_to_truth(reg::poly_predict(quadratic, grid)), " error at 25, 30", extrapolation_error(reg::poly_predict(quadratic, at)), " AIC", quadratic.ols.aic);
  out.writeln("normal family, log coefficients", exponential.coefficients.pull<double>(), " rmse to truth", rmse_to_truth(reg::glm_predict(exponential, grid)), " error at 25, 30", extrapolation_error(reg::glm_predict(exponential, at)), " AIC", exponential.aic);
  out.writeln("median line        coefficients", median.coefficients.pull<double>(), " rmse to truth", rmse_to_truth(reg::quantile_predict(median, grid)), " error at 25, 30", extrapolation_error(reg::quantile_predict(median, at)));
}

Output

truth at x = 25 and 30: 148.413 365.037
straight line      coefficients [-6.671, 2.307]  rmse to truth 5.728  error at 25, 30 [-97.408, -302.497]  AIC 130.653
quadratic          coefficients [3.689, -1.146, 0.182]  rmse to truth 1.700  error at 25, 30 [-59.784, -232.157]  AIC 90.203
normal family, log coefficients [0.598, 0.176]  rmse to truth 0.540  error at 25, 30 [-2.121, -13.201]  AIC 81.430
median line        coefficients [-6.470, 2.263]  rmse to truth 5.705  error at 25, 30 [-98.318, -303.629]

Inside the data the normal-family fit with the log link is closest to the true mean (root mean square error 0.54 against 1.70 for the quadratic and 5.7 for the straight line and the median line), and its AIC, 81.4, is far below those of the quadratic (90.2) and the line (130.7); the three share a Gaussian likelihood, so their AICs are comparable, and the median line’s is not comparable. The difference grows outside the data. At x = 25 and 30 the true means are 148.4 and 365.0, the exponential model is low by 2.1 and 13.2, the quadratic by 60 and 232, and the line by 97 and 302. The quadratic describes the data better than the line inside the range but extrapolates almost as badly. The median line has the straight line’s problem, the wrong shape for the mean. The model with the right form, an exponential mean, does best on every measure shown.

The outlier¶

Every fit above includes the outlier at x = 15. The program refits the straight line, the quadratic and the exponential without it, and shows how far each coefficient set moved. The median line is run on the data with and without it for comparison. A model that responds strongly to one point is being decided by that point.

#include <pluss/ma.h>
#include <pluss/tils/aux/output.h>

namespace reg = pluss::subsp::stats::regression;
using namespace pluss::tils;

int main() {
  OutputEngine out;
  out.print_defaults(PrintOptions{}.fixed(3));
  std::vector<double> xs, ys, xs_clean, ys_clean;
  for (int i = 0; i < 20; ++i) {
    const double value = std::exp(0.5 + 0.18 * i) + 0.6 * (2.0 * std::fmod(i * 0.6180339887498949, 1.0) - 1.0);
    xs.push_back(i);
    ys.push_back(value + (i == 15 ? 8.0 : 0.0));
    if (i != 15) {
      xs_clean.push_back(i);
      ys_clean.push_back(value);
    }
  }
  const auto with = std::make_pair(pluss::make_series(xs, {20}, as_f64()), pluss::make_series(ys, {20}, as_f64()));
  const auto without = std::make_pair(pluss::make_series(xs_clean, {19}, as_f64()), pluss::make_series(ys_clean, {19}, as_f64()));

  auto shift = [&](const char *label, const pluss::Series &a, const pluss::Series &b) {
    out.writeln(label, "with", a.pull<double>(), " without", b.pull<double>(), " largest change", a.sub(b).abs().max().item<double>());
  };
  shift("straight line  ", reg::ols_fit(with.second, with.first).coefficients, reg::ols_fit(without.second, without.first).coefficients);
  shift("quadratic      ", reg::poly_fit(with.second, with.first).ols.coefficients, reg::poly_fit(without.second, without.first).ols.coefficients);
  reg::GLMOptions log_options;
  log_options.link = reg::GLMLink::Log;
  shift("normal, log    ", reg::glm_fit(with.second, with.first, log_options).coefficients, reg::glm_fit(without.second, without.first, log_options).coefficients);
  const auto median_with = reg::quantile_fit(with.second, with.first);
  const auto median_without = reg::quantile_fit(without.second, without.first);
  shift("median line    ", median_with.coefficients, median_without.coefficients);

  // The median line moved by more than the others. Is that the outlier's doing? Score both lines on the full data with the loss the median fit minimises.
  auto loss = [&](const pluss::Series &coefficients) {
    const auto b = coefficients.pull<double>();
    const auto r = with.second.sub(with.first.mul(b[1]).add(b[0]));
    return r.ge(0.0).where(r.mul(0.5), r.mul(-0.5)).sum().item<double>();
  };
  out.writeln("check-function loss on all 20 points: line fitted with the outlier", loss(median_with.coefficients), " line fitted without it", loss(median_without.coefficients));
  out.writeln("the outlier's own residual is", with.second.pull<double>()[15] - (median_with.coefficients.pull<double>()[0] + median_with.coefficients.pull<double>()[1] * 15.0), "against the line fitted with it,", with.second.pull<double>()[15] - (median_without.coefficients.pull<double>()[0] + median_without.coefficients.pull<double>()[1] * 15.0), "against the other");
}

Output

straight line   with [-6.671, 2.307]  without [-6.535, 2.268]  largest change 0.137
quadratic       with [3.689, -1.146, 0.182]  without [3.895, -1.208, 0.183]  largest change 0.206
normal, log     with [0.598, 0.176]  without [0.493, 0.180]  largest change 0.104
median line     with [-6.470, 2.263]  without [-3.574, 1.732]  largest change 2.895
check-function loss on all 20 points: line fitted with the outlier 48.968  line fitted without it 48.968
the outlier's own residual is 4.788 against the line fitted with it, 9.851 against the other

Removing the outlier changes the coefficients of the line, the quadratic and the exponential model by 0.14, 0.21 and 0.10, which is modest. The median line changes by 2.9 (the intercept goes from −6.47 to −3.57 and the slope from 2.263 to 1.732), more than any of the others, but that is not the outlier’s doing: scored on all 20 points, the two median lines have the same check-function loss, 48.968. The loss is flat between them, so the minimiser is not unique for these data, and the optimiser lands on a different member when a point is removed. A median line is robust to how far an outlier lies from the line, not to the non-uniqueness of its minimiser, so for curved data with few points, treat its coefficients as one of several equally good answers.
